title: Classic Problems II: Systems & Follow-ups
summary: Elevators, rate limiters, pub-sub, ride sharing, e-commerce, KV stores, and the follow-up answers that land.

questions.q: Why model the elevator system with an explicit `step()` instead of threads that sleep between floors?
options: Threads are slow
Discrete ticks make scheduling deterministic and unit-testable. A real-time loop can drive `step()` in production
Java elevators don't support threads
To avoid using a TreeSet
questions.explain: Make time explicit (ticks or an injected clock) wherever behaviour depends on time.

questions.q: An elevator at floor 3 is moving UP with stops {5}. New car calls: 1 and 6. In what order does LOOK serve them?
questions.explain: Keep sweeping in the current direction while there are stops ahead (5, 6), then reverse (1).

questions.q: A fixed-window rate limiter allows 100 req/min. What's its well-known weakness?
options: It can't handle multiple users
A burst at the end of one window plus the start of the next allows up to 200 requests within a few seconds
It uses too much memory
It needs a database
questions.explain: Sliding log/counter or token bucket fix the boundary burst. Know the trade-offs: memory vs accuracy vs burst tolerance.

questions.q: In a pub-sub broker with consumer groups, how do several consumers in the **same** group avoid processing the same message?
options: Each consumer keeps its own offset
The group shares one committed offset per topic, and `poll` reads and advances it atomically
Messages are deleted after being read
Consumers coordinate over a separate chat channel
questions.explain: One shared offset per group (or per partition in Kafka) gives work-splitting. Different groups have independent offsets, so each sees everything.

questions.q: Two ride requests arrive at once, and both find driver D as the nearest. What does a correct design guarantee, and how?
options: Nothing. The driver app will reject one
That D is assigned once: selection and marking ON_TRIP happen atomically (one lock, or CAS on the driver's status with fallback to the next candidate)
Both rides get D, and the system fixes it later
Use a random driver to avoid conflicts
questions.explain: It's the same check-then-act hazard as seat booking, just with a driver as the resource.

questions.q: E-commerce: when should stock be deducted to avoid overselling?
options: When the item is added to the cart
Atomically when the order is placed (a reservation), returned on cancel or payment timeout
When the item ships
Nightly by a batch job
questions.explain: Reserve at placement with all-or-nothing across SKUs. Cart-time reservation hurts availability, and ship-time oversells.

questions.q: KV store with nested transactions: what's the efficient way to support ROLLBACK?
options: Deep-copy the whole map on every BEGIN
Keep an undo log per open block that records each key's previous value on its first change in that block, and replay it on rollback
Re-read everything from disk
Disallow nested transactions
questions.explain: Rollback cost is proportional to what changed, not to the store size. COMMIT just discards the logs.

questions.q: Interviewer: "Now persist everything in a database." Best answer for a design built with in-memory maps?
options: "I'd rewrite the services to use SQL directly."

"Services depend on repository interfaces, so I'd add DB-backed implementations. Domain code stays the same, and concurrency moves to DB guarantees like conditional updates, unique constraints or optimistic locking."
"Databases are out of scope for LLD."
"Serialize the maps to a file."
questions.explain: Name the abstraction (repository) that absorbs the change, and the concurrency consequence.

questions.q: "Add a promo code that gives 20% off, capped at ₹100" in a design that already has a `PricingStrategy`. Cleanest change?
options: Add an `if (promo != null)` inside every pricing strategy
A decorator `PromoPricing(inner, code)` that computes the inner price and subtracts min(20%, 100)
A new subclass of every strategy
Store the discounted price in the product table
questions.explain: Decorator composes with any existing strategy, and nothing existing is modified.

questions.q: Which answer to "how would you test this?" signals the strongest design?
options: "I'd test it manually through the UI."

"Time, randomness, payments and notifications are injected, so unit tests use fakes. Concurrency tests start N threads behind a latch and assert invariants like no double booking and conserved money."
"I'd add print statements."
"The QA team handles that."
questions.explain: Testability is a design property, and dependency injection is what enables it.
